newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Single currency remains top priority for EMAC.
newsitem.headline: Single currency remains top priority for EMAC.

text.p: Karl von Wogau, the newly re-elected head of the European Parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee (EMAC), expects to be working on the EU single currency for the rest of this parliament's life.
Preparation for the introduction of the euro will be the main focus of the committee's work until the end of the legislature in June 1999, the German Christian Democrat told Reuters in an interview.
EMAC will have a say in choosing the president and directors of the future European Central Bank, in 1998, and will have a prominent role in monitoring the work of the bank.
The precedent has already been set, with the head of the European Monetary Institute, the bank's predecessor, reporting regularly to the committee.
"The president of the European Central Bank will be independent but (the bank) cannot live in an ivory tower. It will have to explain its decisions to the European people," von Wogau said.
Wim Duisenberg, who is expected to take over as head of the EMI in July, can count on the EMAC chairman's support if he carries through his intentions to stand for leadership of the Central Bank.
"I think he would make a very good candidate," von Wogau, an MEP since 1979, said.
Under von Wogau's chairmanship, the committee will also tackle such questions as double pricing of goods when the euro becomes legal tender.
"I am in favour of a simple rule which would be applied in all the member states because the problems are the same in all the member states," von Wogau said.
He said actually labelling every product with its price in both euros and the national currency during the transition period for the single currency would be costly and generate endless red tape.
It would be enough for shops to display a wall chart indicating the prices of products in both currencies.

As for which member states should qualify for the third phase of European Monetary Union, von Wogau is something of a purist and believes European Union leaders should respect strictly the convergence criteria set out in the Maastricht treaty.
Too loose an interpretation of the criteria would make the markets jittery and push up interest rates, which would particularly harm small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
It could also lead to the German constitutional court challenging Germany's legal right to participate, von Wogau warned.
The prospect of a single currency without Germany worries von Wogau but it is a situation he does not wish to tackle until it actually happens.
"Legally it's possible but practically it would not be possible to go forward without France and Germany," he said.
In the meantime, von Wogau hopes the new Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II) will prove to be a greater success than its predecessor.
This includes giving the Central Bank the power to trigger a currency realignment in good time and allows non-participating currencies to trade in wide fluctuation bands.
"Narrow bands were an invitation to speculation," he said.
VAT HARMONISATION
EMAC will also have the pleasure of handling the debate about harmonising VAT throughout the EU.
Von Wogau declares himself a pragmatist on this issue.
He favours the introduction of an origin-based tax system, as proposed by the European Commission, if it results in less red tape for companies, especially SMEs.
Otherwise, it would be preferable to keep with the current set up -- a transitional halfway house between the new system and the old, destination-based national VAT regimes.
"If (the new system) is based on simple statistical data there will be less red tape. If it has to be run on the basis of figures for individual sales the red tape would not be diminished," he said.
TELECOMMUNICATIONS

During the lulls in the debate about the euro, EMAC will have to tackle two major draft directives in the telecommunications sector, one on interconnections, COM(95)379, the other on rules for licences, COM(95)545.
The interconnection directive is heading for a conciliation committee that will try to iron out differences between the parliament and Council.
The work must be completed in time for the January 1, 1998, deadline for liberalisation of the sector.

"I think its's important that we make sure that the barriers for the new entrants (to the telecoms market) are not too high and that universal service is regulated in a way that corresponds to the needs of this special service," the Christian Democrat said.
Cooperation between national telecoms regulators was vital too, he added.
There is little the parliament can do to stop the member states dawdling over the full transposition into national law of the new EU laws on telecoms liberalisation.
But von Wogau believes pressure from outside competitors, such as America's AT&T, will spur EU governments into action.
SMEs/CUSTOMS
Defending the interests of SMEs is an issue close to von Wogau's heart. Another is getting the EU's external customs posts to operate in a more effective and coordinated fashion.
Von Wogau, the author of a recent report on improving EU customs, wants to see all paperwork at the EU's entry points replaced by a single computerised system.

Protests from the European Commission about the cost of such an arrangement get short shrift from the German MEP, especially when the EU's executive appears to him to be quite happy to spend money on electronically linking the member states' health systems and other services.

Computerising customs services now was an absolute priority, von Wogau insisted, because protecting the EU's external borders and abolishing all internal ones was one of the EU's main goals and responsibilities.
